notes: Clear procedural ruling on adjourning admitted contempt proceedings pending criminal cases.

enrichment.short_title: Adjourning Housing Act 1996 contempt after admitted breach
key_facts: Stafford Borough Council obtained without-notice section 152 injunctions with powers of arrest against tenants and associates on a council estate following anti-social behaviour.
On 5 August 2002, when the injunctions were served, the Haynes family and Sandra Anderson reacted violently, assaulted process servers, and resisted arrest.
All three defendants appeared on 9 August 2002, were legally represented, and admitted the factual allegations in the committal applications.
Judge Mitchell nevertheless adjourned the committal applications indefinitely until any criminal proceedings concluded, any further breach occurred, or the court restored the matter.
Benjamin Haynes was later prosecuted for assault, but no prosecutions were brought against Gary Haynes or Sandra Anderson.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant local authority's appeal against part of a county court order adjourning committal proceedings after defendants admitted breach of anti-social behaviour injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the county court for prompt determination of the committal applications.
enrichment.ratio: Although a judge may adjourn contempt proceedings in a proper case, it is ordinarily wrong to adjourn a properly brought committal application against the applicant's wishes to an indefinite future date, especially where breaches are admitted, there is no real risk of prejudice to parallel criminal proceedings, and contempt proceedings should be dealt with swiftly and separately from criminal punishment.
legal_issues: Whether a judge may adjourn committal proceedings indefinitely pending possible criminal proceedings
Whether housing officers serving injunctions are protected by section 152 of the Housing Act 1996
Whether admitted contempt proceedings should be determined promptly despite parallel criminal process

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence on golf club lease rent review
key_facts: Eagle Major Ltd retained Bentleys Stokes & Lowless to act on its acquisition of a 100-year lease of land at Studley Wood, Oxfordshire, where it spent about £1.6m building a golf club.
The lease contained an RPI-linked rent review and an alternative market rent review under which improvements made pursuant to tenant obligations were not disregarded.
Because the tenant was obliged to construct the golf course, a market rent review could assess rent on the value of the developed site rather than undeveloped land with planning permission.
The claimant alleged Miss Collett negligently introduced the market rent review mechanism without explaining that the tenant could end up paying rent on its own capital expenditure.
The claim was worth about £750,000; the deputy master refused strike-out and summary judgment, and the solicitors appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a deputy master's refusal to strike out or grant summary judgment in a solicitor negligence claim concerning a commercial lease rent review clause.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the claim may proceed to trial on negligence, breach of contract, and section 14A limitation issues.
enrichment.ratio: At an interlocutory stage the court should not conduct a mini-trial or reject a claim as fanciful where correspondence and witness evidence raise a real dispute about what the tenant understood and whether the solicitor adequately explained a rent review clause with potentially drastic commercial consequences.
legal_issues: Whether the negligence and breach of contract claim had any real prospect of success
Whether the claim was time-barred from the date of the lease or only from later discovery
Whether section 14A Limitation Act 1980 postponed the limitation period
Construction and effect of the market rent review disregard provisions

enrichment.short_title: Youth court venue for robbery by 14-year-olds
key_facts: Three 14-year-olds were charged with robbery or attempted robbery before Sheffield Youth Court in July 2002.
C and D, of good character, were alleged to have robbed a schoolfriend of £2 after pushing, punching, and kicking her.
N, with one previous conviction, was alleged to have attempted to rob a motorbike owner using sustained violence and a head-butt.
The youth court declined jurisdiction under section 24(1), committing all three for Crown Court trial on the basis that a section 91 custodial sentence might be possible.
The claimants sought judicial review, arguing conflicting High Court authorities on the proper test for venue and review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review applications to quash Sheffield Youth Court decisions committing 14-year-old defendants for trial in the Crown Court on robbery-related charges.
enrichment.outcome: Decision to commit C and D quashed; application in respect of N dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A youth court should commit a defendant under section 24(1) only if it considers there is a real possibility of a section 91 sentence, taking into account undisputed mitigation but not the general unsuitability of the Crown Court as a separate discretionary factor; on judicial review the High Court may interfere if the youth court's decision was wrong, not merely different from that which the reviewing judge would have made.
legal_issues: What factors a youth court may consider under section 24(1) of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980
Whether commitment is mandatory once a section 91 sentence is considered possible
The test for judicial review of a youth court venue decision
Whether local sentencing guidelines and undisclosed legal advice invalidated the decisions

notes: VAT capital goods case stayed for ECJ reference; no final merits determination.

enrichment.short_title: VAT capital goods adjustment on split land disposal
key_facts: Centralan Properties Ltd bought the Harrington Building in Preston for £6.5m plus VAT and leased it back to the University of Central Lancashire.

In the third adjustment interval Centralan disposed of its interest by granting a 999-year reversionary lease to a connected company for a £6.37m premium and transferring the freehold reversion to the University for £1,000.
The long lease was an exempt supply between connected persons; the freehold transfer was standard-rated.

Customs contended Regulation 115(3) required apportionment between the supplies, creating a liability of about £796,090; Centralan argued only the taxable transfer mattered, limiting liability to about £944.
The VAT and Duties Tribunal rejected Centralan's case and ordered apportionment; Centralan appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the VAT and Duties Tribunal on the construction of Regulation 115(3) following a capital goods adjustment on disposal of land by two linked transactions.
enrichment.outcome: Proceedings stayed and a reference to the European Court of Justice proposed on the interpretation of Article 20(3) of the Sixth Directive.
enrichment.ratio: Where the proper construction of Regulation 115(3) depends on the meaning of Article 20(3) in relation to successive supplies of immovable property and no ECJ authority provides sufficient guidance, a national court should refer the question rather than resolve a large, generally important VAT dispute on an uncertain basis.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 115(3) applies to one supply or requires apportionment between multiple supplies in the same interval
How Article 20(3) of the Sixth Directive applies to disposals of immovable property by connected transactions
Whether a national court should make a reference to the ECJ
Whether pre-ordained two-stage land transactions should be treated as fully taxed, fully exempt, or apportioned

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside sovereign immunity after aircraft perjury
key_facts: Kuwait Airways Corporation sued Iraqi Airways Corporation for wrongful interference with ten aircraft seized during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The House of Lords held in 1995 that Iraqi Airways had sovereign immunity for removing the aircraft but not for retention and use after Iraqi Resolution 369 on 17 September 1990.
Kuwait Airways later brought a fraud action alleging that Iraqi Airways witnesses falsely told earlier courts that, before 17 September, only basic maintenance was performed.
Fresh documentary evidence indicated repainting, re-registration, insurance, recruitment of engineers, and preparation for commercial use from early August 1990.
The judge found that Mr Saffi and Mr Abbo gave perjured evidence and that Iraqi Airways had begun absorbing the fleet before Resolution 369.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial court action to set aside earlier House of Lords and trial findings on sovereign immunity for the period between 9 August and 17 September 1990 on the basis of perjured evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Perjury and material change in the nature of the case established; sovereign immunity should not bind Kuwait Airways for Iraqi Airways' activities from 9 August 1990 onwards.
enrichment.ratio: Where fresh evidence shows that witnesses representing a state-owned corporation knowingly gave false testimony that underpinned an earlier sovereign immunity finding, and the true facts show commercial absorption of misappropriated aircraft rather than merely maintenance related to seizure, the earlier immunity analysis for the interim period is fundamentally changed and the separate entity's acts are not acts jure imperii.
legal_issues: Whether a judgment may be set aside for fraud based on perjured evidence
Whether new evidence entirely changes the sovereign immunity analysis under section 14(2) State Immunity Act 1978
Whether pre-Resolution 369 conduct amounted to commercial rather than governmental acts
Whether corporate officers' perjury may be attributed to Iraqi Airways

enrichment.short_title: Nightclub promoters and lease sharing covenant
key_facts: Mean Fiddler Holdings operated The Complex nightclub on leasehold premises compulsorily acquired by Islington London Borough in December 1999.

From late 1998 the tenant used external promoters on regular weekly nights who controlled programming, advertising, and admission revenue while the tenant retained control of the premises, security, bars, and equipment.
The compensating authority argued this arrangement breached clause 23(a) against sharing occupation of part of the property.
The Lands Tribunal held there was no breach on a preliminary issue; the authority appealed on a point of law.
A separate section 5(4) Land Compensation Act point on unlawful use was not before the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from a Lands Tribunal preliminary issue determining whether use of external promoters breached an alienation covenant in a compulsory purchase compensation reference.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tenant's arrangements did not breach clause 23(a) of the lease.
enrichment.ratio: Whether external promoters share occupation under a covenant against sharing possession or occupation of part of the demised premises depends on whether a third party has been allowed such control of the property itself as to amount to occupation; where the tenant remains exclusively responsible for the premises and the promoters control only the event, there is no breach even in a regular weekly arrangement.
legal_issues: Construction of a covenant against sharing occupation of part of leased premises
Whether external nightclub promoters were sharing occupation or merely participating in the tenant's business
Whether the control test or business-use test governs clause 23(a)
Relevance of permitted user as a licensed social club and discotheque

key_facts: Dr Das applied under section 41A(10) of the Medical Act 1983 to terminate the GMC Interim Orders Committee's suspension of his registration.
The suspension had followed earlier conditions on his practice and was due to expire in April 2003, with a full Committee for Professional Performance hearing listed for March 2003.

He alleged Article 3 ECHR breach, factual error by the IOC, and improper political or resource-based motives.
A late adjournment request based on a family emergency was considered but would not have altered the outcome.

enrichment.ratio: On an application to terminate an interim suspension under section 41A(10), the court gives due weight to the GMC's specialist assessment and will not substitute its own view unless there is a proper legal basis to interfere; unsupported allegations of factual error, political motive, or Article 3 breach do not justify lifting suspension.

enrichment.short_title: Henderson abuse and later fraud claims
key_facts: Dexter Ltd was used in a fraudulent scheme to obtain a £2 million bank advance based on forged documents relating to a worthless aircraft engine.
In 1999 Dexter sued Martin Vlieland-Boddy alone and obtained a £2 million judgment after he abandoned his defence at trial.
Further tracing revealed payments to Clive Vlieland-Boddy and Edwina Harley; a second action against Mrs Harley alone was struck out for want of jurisdiction under the Brussels Convention.
In February 2002 Dexter commenced fresh proceedings against Clive Vlieland-Boddy, Mrs Harley, and others for dishonest assistance, knowing receipt, and conspiracy.
The first and fourth defendants applied to strike out the claims as an abuse of process under Henderson v Henderson.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against refusal to strike out claims in later proceedings as an abuse of process following an earlier successful action against one conspirator.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; the later claims may proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Johnson v Gore Wood, the question is a broad merits-based assessment whether later proceedings against different defendants involve unjust harassment; failure to join a defendant in an earlier action does not necessarily make a later claim abusive, especially where the claimant initially pursued the obvious primary wrongdoer and only later obtained evidence against others.
legal_issues: Application of the rule in Henderson v Henderson to successive actions against different defendants
Whether Dexter should have joined Clive Vlieland-Boddy and Edwina Harley in the first action
Whether continuation of a freezing order without prompt fresh proceedings was abusive

notes: Committal sentence quashed for procedural unfairness; breach findings upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe committal sentence for lorry obstruction
key_facts: Marshall Properties obtained without-notice injunctions requiring Mr Rothschild to remove a lorry obstructing a level crossing and not to interfere with a claimed right of way.
After the lorry remained, committal proceedings were heard before Judge Darlow in June 2002.
On 10 June the judge told Mr Rothschild to bring an overnight bag if the lorry was still present on 12 June, before the committal case was fully heard.
On 12 June the judge found contempt proved, rejected a sham sale of the vehicle, and immediately committed Mr Rothschild to three months' imprisonment without hearing submissions on penalty.
Mr Rothschild purged his contempt two days later and the underlying dispute was later determined in December 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal, out of time, against county court orders refusing recusal and refusing to set aside an injunction, with the live issue being the safety of a committal sentence for breach of injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; breach findings upheld but the three-month imprisonment sentence quashed and no penalty imposed.
enrichment.ratio: In committal proceedings for civil contempt the judge must not indicate a predetermined sentence before the case is fully heard, must give the contemnor an opportunity to be heard on penalty, and should consider a suspended sentence where the primary purpose is to secure compliance; procedural errors of this kind render an immediate custodial sentence unsafe even where breach is proved.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have recused himself for prior knowledge of the right of way
Whether committal for breach of a without-notice injunction was proved
Whether telling the contemnor to bring an overnight bag showed predetermination
Whether failure to hear submissions on penalty invalidated the sentence

notes: Leading construction of customs regulations exclusion in Institute War Clauses.

enrichment.short_title: War risks exclusion for drug smuggling detention
key_facts: Sunport Shipping insured the Kleovoulos of Rhodes under Institute War and Strikes Clauses including a constructive total loss provision after six months' detainment.
On arrival in Aliveri, Greece in August 1998, a large quantity of cocaine was discovered hidden in a sea chest below the waterline.
The master and crew were charged under Greek narcotics law and the vessel was detained; abandonment was rejected after six months.
The vessel was eventually released in May 1999 and sold for far less than the agreed insured value of US$8 million.
Underwriters relied on clause 4.1.5 excluding loss arising from detainment by reason of infringement of customs or trading regulations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against dismissal of a war risks constructive total loss claim for a vessel detained after discovery of drugs on board.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the exclusion in clause 4.1.5 applied and underwriters were not liable for the constructive total loss.
enrichment.ratio: In the international context of the Institute War Clauses, 'customs regulations' includes laws prohibiting import of controlled goods as well as duty-levying rules; where detention for at least six months proximately arises from unlawful importation of drugs discovered on the vessel, the constructive total loss is excluded even if the crew were later acquitted.
legal_issues: Whether Greek narcotics import prohibitions are 'customs regulations' within Institute War Clauses 4.1.5
Whether The Anita gives a settled meaning to the exclusion clause
Whether six months' detainment was proximately caused by infringement of customs regulations
Whether acquittal of the crew broke the chain of causation
